questions.prompt: Distinguish precision from accuracy in a length measurement.

marking.point: Precision concerns agreement between repeated readings.
Accuracy concerns closeness to an accepted / true value.

questions.prompt: A block has mass (0.240 ± 0.003) kg and volume (8.0 ± 0.2) × 10⁻⁵ m³. Calculate its density, ignoring uncertainty for this part.

marking.point: ρ = m / V.

questions.prompt: Use the conservative sum-of-percentage-uncertainties method to estimate the density uncertainty for the same block. Express the result with an absolute uncertainty.

marking.point: For a quotient, add the percentage uncertainties.
Mass uncertainty = 1.25%; volume uncertainty = 2.5%; total = 3.75%.
Absolute uncertainty = 3000 × 0.0375 = 112.5 kg m⁻³.
A suitable report is (3.00 ± 0.11) × 10³ kg m⁻³; uncertainty is an estimate, not a correction.

questions.prompt: Every reading from a balance is 0.010 kg too high. Explain why taking ten readings does not remove this problem and propose a correction.

marking.point: A constant offset is a systematic error.

mastery.why: Leading zeros do not count; the trailing zero after the decimal does.

tasks.lessonTitle: Friction, Tension and Motion on Slopes

questions.prompt: Distinguish static and kinetic friction.

marking.point: Static friction opposes impending relative sliding and adjusts up to a maximum.
Kinetic friction acts when surfaces are sliding; its magnitude is modelled by μₖN.

questions.prompt: A 5.0 kg block slides on a horizontal surface with μₖ = 0.20. Find the friction magnitude. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻².

marking.point: fₖ = μₖN; N = mg for this horizontal case.

questions.prompt: A 6.0 kg block slides down a 30° slope with μₖ = 0.15. Calculate its acceleration.

marking.point: N = mg cos θ; fₖ = μₖmg cos θ acts upslope.
Net downslope force = mg sin θ − μₖmg cos θ.
a = 9.8(sin 30° − 0.15 cos 30°) = 3.63 m s⁻² downslope.
Mass cancels in this ideal model; do not use N = mg on the slope.

questions.prompt: A stationary block has a maximum static friction of 18 N. A 10 N horizontal pull is applied. Explain its friction and motion.

marking.point: Static friction adjusts to 10 N, opposing the pull.
The maximum 18 N is a limit, not the friction in every situation.
Net horizontal force is zero, so the block remains at rest.

questions.prompt: Define momentum and impulse and state their connection.

marking.point: Momentum is p = mv, a vector.
Impulse is the net-force time integral / FΔt for a constant force and equals change in momentum.

marking.point: J = Δp = m(v − u).

questions.prompt: The stopping time is increased from 0.010 s to 0.060 s. Calculate the magnitudes of the average forces and their ratio.

marking.point: |Favg| = |Δp| / Δt for the same momentum change.
Short stop: 1.5 / 0.010 = 150 N.
Long stop: 1.5 / 0.060 = 25 N; short / long = 6.0.
Increasing stop time reduces average force for the same impulse; peak force need not equal average force.

questions.prompt: Explain how an airbag can reduce injury without reducing the passenger’s required momentum change to zero.

questions.prompt: State the condition for momentum conservation and distinguish it from kinetic-energy conservation.

marking.point: Total momentum is conserved if external impulse on the system is negligible.

questions.prompt: A 1.5 kg trolley at 4.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 2.5 kg trolley and they stick. Find their common velocity.

marking.point: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = (m₁ + m₂)v.
v = 1.5 m s⁻¹ in the first trolley’s initial direction.

questions.prompt: For that collision, calculate the kinetic energy transformed into other forms.

marking.point: Initial KE = ½m₁u₁² + ½m₂u₂².
Initial KE = ½ × 1.5 × 4.0² = 12.0 J.
Final KE = ½ × 4.0 × 1.5² = 4.5 J; decrease = 7.5 J.
The decrease becomes internal energy, sound or deformation; total energy remains conserved.

questions.prompt: Explain why equal and opposite collision forces do not imply equal accelerations for unequal masses.

marking.point: The interaction forces have equal magnitudes by Newton’s third law.

questions.prompt: Explain why a fixed-frequency classical cyclotron becomes unsuitable as massive particles become strongly relativistic.

The revolution frequency decreases from the low-speed qB/(2πm) value by the γ factor.
Particles lose synchronisation with an unchanged accelerating frequency; timing / field control must be adjusted.

questions.prompt: Distinguish cosmological redshift from a change in the locally measured vacuum speed of light.

marking.point: Cosmological redshift is the increase in light wavelength as the universe expands during propagation.
Local vacuum light speed remains c; redshift does not mean light travels locally more slowly.

questions.prompt: A spectral line emitted at 500 nm is observed at 525 nm. Calculate redshift z.

marking.point: z = (λobserved − λemitted)/λemitted.

questions.prompt: Use the low-redshift approximations v ≈ cz and v = H₀d, with c = 3.0 × 10⁵ km s⁻¹ and H₀ = 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, to estimate distance for z = 0.050.

marking.point: d = v/H₀.
This simplified estimate assumes Hubble flow and low redshift; peculiar motion and a full cosmological model are omitted.

questions.prompt: Give three distinct observations supporting the hot Big Bang model and briefly connect each to the model.

marking.point: Large-scale redshift–distance relation supports expansion from a denser earlier state.
Cosmic microwave background supports a hot early universe that cooled as it expanded.
Light-element abundance patterns broadly agree with early-universe nucleosynthesis predictions.
